C005.subject: Low-skilled immigration
C005.object: employment opportunities for native workers in complementary roles
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Low-skilled immigration employment opportunities for native workers in complementary roles]

[PATH:empirical] Panel data analysis of low-skilled labor markets in U.S. metropolitan areas (e.g., using Current Population Survey or American Community Survey) during periods of low-skilled labor demand growth (e.g., 1990s tech boom, 2010s construction recovery) to measure changes in native employment in complementary roles (e.g., team leads, quality control, logistics coordination). — Directly tests the causal effect of low-skilled immigration on native complementary employment under the specified temporal and geographic conditions, controlling for local demand shocks.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical models of labor market complementarity (e.g., Ottaviano & Peri 2012, or Dustmann, Frattini & Preston 2013) applied to flexible labor markets, simulating the impact of low-skilled immigrant inflows on native job specialization and task reassignment. — Provides a formal framework to predict when and why complementarity effects dominate substitution effects, especially in flexible labor markets during demand growth, offering testable predictions for empirical work.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing studies on low-skilled immigration and native employment outcomes in OECD countries with flexible labor markets (e.g., UK, Australia, Canada) during periods of rising low-skilled labor demand (e.g., pre-2008 construction booms). — Synthesizes available evidence to assess the overall direction and magnitude of the effect, identifying whether the hypothesis holds across different contexts and methodological approaches.

qualifier.temporal: during periods of low-skilled labor demand growth
qualifier.geographic: in developed economies with flexible labor markets

C006.subject: Low-skilled immigration
C006.object: wages for native workers without a high school diploma
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Low-skilled immigration wages for native workers without a high school diploma]

[PATH:empirical] Borjas, G.J. (2003). 'The Labor Demand Curve Is Downward Sloping: Reexamining the Impact of Immigration on the Labor Market.' Quarterly Journal of Economics, 118(4), 1335-1374. — This seminal study uses a skill-cell approach to estimate the effect of low-skilled immigration on native wages, providing evidence that immigration reduces wages for competing native workers, which would refute the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Card, D. (2009). 'Immigration and Inequality.' American Economic Review, 99(2), 1-21. — Card's analysis of the Mariel Boatlift and other natural experiments suggests that low-skilled immigration has minimal negative wage effects on native workers, and may even increase wages through complementarities, supporting the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Ottaviano, G.I.P., & Peri, G. (2012). 'Rethinking the Effect of Immigration on Wages.' Journal of the European Economic Association, 10(1), 152-197. — This paper develops a theoretical model distinguishing between perfect and imperfect substitution of immigrant and native labor, showing that low-skilled immigration can raise native wages by increasing demand for complementary skills, offering a mechanism to confirm the hypothesis.

C007.subject: High-skilled immigration
C007.object: innovation and productivity in high-skilled sectors
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: High-skilled immigration innovation and productivity in high-skilled sectors]

[PATH:empirical] National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) working papers on immigration and innovation, e.g., 'The Impact of High-Skilled Immigration on Firm-Level Productivity' — Provides firm-level panel data analysis linking H-1B visa holders to patenting rates and R&D output in U.S. tech sectors, directly testing the causal effect on innovation and productivity.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of cross-country studies on high-skilled immigration and total factor productivity (TFP) in OECD economies, e.g., from Journal of Economic Geography or Research Policy — Synthesizes findings across multiple OECD countries to assess whether the positive effect holds consistently or is moderated by institutional factors, addressing geographic scope and temporal qualifiers.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical model of knowledge spillovers and labor market competition in high-skilled sectors, e.g., from Borjas (2005) or Peri (2012) extensions — Formalizes mechanisms through which immigrant scientists and engineers either complement native workers (boosting innovation) or substitute them (reducing incentives), helping to interpret conflicting empirical results.

qualifier.geographic: United States and other OECD countries

C008.subject: High-skilled immigration
C008.object: wages for native workers through substitution effects in concentrated labor markets
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: High-skilled immigration wages for native workers through substitution effects in concentrated labor markets]

[PATH:empirical] Borjas (2003) 'The Labor Demand Curve is Downward Sloping: Reexamining the Impact of Immigration on the Labor Market' and subsequent updates using ACS data through 2020 — Provides a direct empirical framework for estimating wage effects of immigration by skill group and geographic area, with methods to isolate substitution effects in concentrated labor markets.

[PATH:literature] Peri, G. & Sparber, C. (2009) 'Task Specialization, Immigration, and Wages' and related work on task-based substitution vs. complementarity — Offers a theoretical and empirical counterpoint, arguing that high-skilled immigrants often complement native workers through task specialization, which could refute the substitution-driven wage depression hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Kerr, S.P. & Kerr, W.R. (2011) 'Economic Impacts of Immigration: A Survey' and linked firm-level studies using H-1B visa data — Reviews firm-level evidence on how high-skilled immigration affects wages and employment, focusing on concentrated tech labor markets; can confirm or refute substitution effects by examining within-firm wage dynamics.

C009.subject: Immigration
C009.object: wages for native workers in technology sectors due to complementary skills
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Immigration wages for native workers in technology sectors due to complementary skills]

[PATH:empirical] Borjas, G. J. (2014). Immigration Economics. Harvard University Press. Also recent papers using variation in H-1B visa lotteries to estimate wage effects on native tech workers. — This literature directly tests the impact of high-skilled immigration on native wages, using quasi-experimental methods (e.g., lottery-based allocation) to isolate causal effects. It can confirm or refute whether complementary skills lead to wage increases in tech sectors.

[PATH:empirical] Peri, G., & Sparber, C. (2009). 'Task Specialization, Immigration, and Wages.' American Economic Journal: Applied Economics, 1(3), 135-169. — This study provides evidence on how immigration shifts task specialization, potentially raising wages for native workers who perform complementary tasks. It is directly relevant to the hypothesis that complementary skills in technology sectors increase native wages.

[PATH:literature] National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2017). 'The Economic and Fiscal Consequences of Immigration.' Report summarizing multiple studies and meta-analyses. — This comprehensive review synthesizes evidence across many studies, including those on technology sectors, and can help assess the overall weight of evidence for or against the hypothesis, especially regarding complementary skills and wage effects.

C010.subject: Immigration
C010.object: wages for native workers in local labor markets with high concentrations of low-skilled immigrants, even after demand-side adjustments
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Immigration wages for native workers in local labor markets with high concentrations of low-skilled immigrants, even after demand-side adjustments]

[PATH:empirical] Card (1990) 'The Impact of the Mariel Boatlift on the Miami Labor Market' and subsequent replications (e.g., Peri & Yasenov, 2019) — This quasi-experimental study directly examines wage effects of a sudden low-skilled immigrant influx on native workers in a local labor market. Re-analyses with updated methods and data can test whether the original finding of no negative wage effects holds under demand-side adjustments, providing critical evidence for or against the hypothesis.

[PATH:empirical] Borjas (2003) 'The Labor Demand Curve Is Downward Sloping: Reexamining the Impact of Immigration on the Labor Market' and related spatial correlation studies using decennial Census/ACS data — Borjas' work uses a national skill-cell approach (education-experience groups) to estimate wage effects, which contrasts with local labor market studies. Comparing results from this methodology (which often finds negative effects) with local-area studies can clarify whether the hypothesis holds when accounting for endogenous labor demand shifts and native mobility responses.

[PATH:literature] Dustmann, Schönberg, & Stuhler (2016) 'The Impact of Immigration: Why Do Studies Reach Such Different Results?' — This comprehensive review synthesizes methodological differences (e.g., spatial vs. national approaches, treatment of endogenous responses) that explain conflicting findings. It can help identify which empirical designs and data sources are most likely to confirm or refute the hypothesis, and what additional controls (e.g., demand-side adjustments) are needed to resolve the dispute.
